About your practitioner

Youwei Feng — Registered Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioner & Registered Acupuncturist, Ontario, Canada

Before practising in Canada, Youwei Feng spent over 30 years as a Chief Physician （主任醫師） at a Grade-A tertiary （三甲） hospital in China, with deep clinical and theoretical expertise in both Traditional Chinese Medicine and Western medicine — training that informs both this assessment and the clinic's lab and imaging interpretation service.

This assessment was prepared by Harmony TCM Wellness. A questionnaire can point in a direction, but real pattern differentiation happens in the clinic room — through conversation, pulse and tongue diagnosis, and your full health history. If your result concerns you, or you would like a formula prescribed properly for your constitution, book an in-person consultation. Acupuncture treatments at the clinic may be covered by extended health benefits, and direct billing is available.

Traditional Chinese Medicine is a regulated health profession in Ontario. For the regulator’s own introduction to TCM, see About Traditional Chinese Medicine — College of Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioners and Acupuncturists of Ontario (CTCMPAO).

Tongue photo 舌苔照片

Natural light, no flash, no filters. Best in the morning before eating, drinking coffee or brushing your teeth — stick your tongue out fully and let it relax.

Imaging 影像資料

Lab results 實驗室結果

Supporting Women's Health at Every Stage of Life 女性健康

Today, two patient stories touched our hearts and reminded us why we are so passionate about what we do.

A Special Milestone on the Fertility Journey

One of our patients had been trying to conceive for several years before coming to our clinic for acupuncture support as part of her fertility journey. She recently shared the wonderful news that she is now over six weeks pregnant!

We were truly delighted to hear her news and feel honoured to have been part of her journey. With the joy and excitement of early pregnancy also come some understandable nerves. She continues to visit our clinic for relaxation and support during this special time.

A Personal Experience During Perimenopause

Another patient navigating perimenopause shared that she had not experienced a menstrual period for six months. She noticed that her period returned three days after an acupuncture session.

Every woman's body and health journey is unique. These experiences remind us of the importance of listening, providing individualized care, and supporting women through different stages of life.

Fertility and infertility care is one of our clinic's specialties.

A Gentle Reminder: These are individual patient experiences and should not be interpreted as evidence that acupuncture caused these outcomes. Results vary from person to person, and no particular outcome is guaranteed. This post is for general informational purposes only and is not a substitute for medical advice or care from your healthcare provider.

Celebrating 6 Years — Thank You 六週年

Time flies. Our Goderich clinic opened on October 1, 2020, and our London clinic followed in March 2024 — six years of care and counting. For six years, we have treated every patient with dedication and wholehearted care: staying late for urgent cases, never closing even on the snowiest days — all to relieve pain and restore health.

Thank you to everyone who left us a kind review on Google; we are deeply moved that so many of you anonymously shared your valuable feedback on the Sun Life platform — your trust means the world to us; and thank you to the 219 of you who rated us 9.8 out of 10 on ClinicSense — we are grateful for every single score.

Individual experiences; results vary from person to person.

A Family Legacy: Healing Through the 1932 Epidemic 家傳醫道

A story from our family's own history — the reason healing has always been our calling.

In the autumn and winter of 1932 — the 21st year of the Republic of China — an epidemic swept through our hometown. My great-grandfather, assisted by my grandfather, treated nearly a hundred patients. Not one was lost.

For nearly a month they worked day and night, forgetting sleep and meals, until every patient had recovered.

Grateful villagers quietly organized a gift of two plaques, delivered on a day of drums and firecrackers. The first reads 壽世回春 — "Rejuvenation and Longevity." The second reads 妙手回春 — "Skillful Hands Restoring Youth."

This story comes from our family's own history, shared here as it was passed down to us.

A Record-Breaking Comeback: Ben's Story 力量舉

Ben Worsell is a powerlifter in the M60–69 division. On November 7, 2026, at the WRPF Nationals, he went nine for nine — squat 215 kg, bench press 160 kg, deadlift 227.5 kg — for a 602.5 kg total, breaking world records in his age group.

Ben has been a patient at our clinic for nearly three years. After a total knee replacement, he worked his way back to the platform — and then some. When the competition was over, he came straight to the clinic and hung his medal around his acupuncturist Youwei Feng's neck, in thanks for nearly three years of treatment.

⚠ Please read before you begin — educational tool only, not a diagnosis

This self-assessment is provided for health education only. It is a simplified questionnaire based on TCM pattern-differentiation theory; it is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace an in-person consultation, which also relies on pulse-taking, tongue inspection and a full health history. Herbal formulas are classical references from the TCM literature — do not prepare, purchase or take any herbal formula on the basis of this page. Herbs can interact with prescription medication and some are unsafe in pregnancy or without professional preparation. Any formula should be prescribed and adjusted by a registered TCM practitioner who has assessed you in person. If you have a medical condition, are pregnant, or take prescription medication, speak with your physician or a registered practitioner first.

Winter Wellness, the TCM Way

In TCM, winter belongs to the Kidney system — a season for storing, resting, and warming from within. These are general habits, not prescriptions: your own pattern decides the details.

Eat — warm from within

  • Favour warm, cooked food: soups, stews, and congee; ginger, cinnamon, lamb, walnuts, black sesame, black beans, and black rice.
  • Go easy on raw and cold food and iced drinks — cold injures Yang, and winter is when Yang most needs protecting.
  • Eat at regular times and avoid heavy late-night meals. If you tend to feel hot, dry, or restless, heavy tonics can backfire — warming should match your constitution.

Dress — guard the gates

  • Keep the head, neck, lower back, and feet warm — in TCM, cold is said to enter through the feet.
  • Dress in layers so you can adjust between indoors and out, and keep the waist and knees covered.
  • Wear warm socks or slippers indoors rather than letting your feet stay cold on the floor.

Home — store and rest

  • Sleep earlier and rise a little later — the classic winter advice is "early to bed, late to rise, waiting for the sunlight."
  • Keep rooms warm but aired: open windows briefly each day, and ease dry air with a humidifier or a bowl of water near the heat.
  • A warm bath or shower before bed helps; avoid getting chilled right after sweating.

Out & about — move gently

  • Exercise after sunrise when you can. Walking, tai chi, and stretching are ideal — move until lightly warm, not drenched in sweat.
  • On cold mornings, warm up indoors first and protect your head and neck outside.
  • Watch your footing on ice — falls are the classic winter injury. Wear steady shoes and take short steps.

Common TCM & acupuncture questions

Does acupuncture hurt?

Most people feel little or nothing — the needles are very fine. You may notice a dull ache, heaviness, or tingling, which practitioners call deqi. If you are nervous, say so; treatment can start very gently.

Is acupuncture safe?

When performed by a registered practitioner using sterile, single-use needles, serious side effects are rare. Minor bruising or soreness can happen. Tell the practitioner if you are pregnant, take blood thinners, or have a bleeding disorder — some points and techniques are adjusted or avoided.

What is pattern differentiation?

Instead of treating one symptom alone, TCM looks at the whole picture — sleep, digestion, mood, tongue, and pulse — to identify the underlying pattern, such as Qi Deficiency or Damp-Heat. That is why this site's assessment asks about more than your main complaint.

What do people commonly seek acupuncture for?

Pain (back, neck, joints), headaches, stress and sleep problems, digestive complaints, and women's reproductive health — including fertility support, painful periods, and breech presentation, where moxibustion is traditionally used in late pregnancy to encourage the baby to turn — are common reasons people seek acupuncture. Acupuncture does not replace medical care — serious or worsening symptoms should be checked by a physician.

How many sessions will I need?

It depends on the problem. Recent issues may improve in a few visits; long-standing ones usually take longer. The practitioner reassesses as you go rather than fixing a number in advance.

How often should I come?

Generally once a week, with a reassessment after 5 to 8 weeks. The exact frequency depends on your individual condition — the practitioner adjusts the plan based on how you respond.

What happens at a first visit?

A conversation about your health history, plus pulse and tongue diagnosis, then treatment. Bring a list of medications and any recent lab or imaging reports if you have them.

What should I do after treatment?

Rest a little, drink water, and avoid heavy exertion, alcohol, and getting chilled right after. Mild tiredness or soreness can happen and usually passes quickly.

What about cupping and moxibustion?

Cupping uses suction cups and can leave temporary round marks that fade within days. Moxibustion warms points with mugwort. The practitioner decides whether either suits your pattern.

Does insurance cover acupuncture?

Many extended health plans cover it, and the clinic offers direct billing. Check your own plan's coverage and limits.

Do I have to choose between TCM and Western medicine?

No. Many patients use both. Tell each provider what the other is doing, especially about herbs and medications, so nothing interacts.

General education only — not a diagnosis and not a substitute for medical advice. If you have a specific condition, book an assessment and discuss it with the practitioner.
